# 1 Maccabees Chapter 8 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Codex Sinaiticus, 1 Maccabees 8

---

## Council Notes

**On the Roman Republic as seen from the East (vv.1-16):** This passage is the most remarkable in the chapter — and among the most interesting in the entire Deuterocanon. The author presents the Roman Republic through Jewish eyes circa 160 BCE: their power is acknowledged, their civic virtue admired (no king, no purple), their senate praised. The historical context is 161 BCE, and the description — though partly idealized — reflects genuine admiration. In retrospect, the description is both accurate (the Republic was at its zenith) and naive about what Rome would become. All translators must render this with the earnest admiration of the original, not ironic distance.

**On "senate" (v.15):** The Greek *sunkletos* = the Roman Senate. All translators preserve "senate." The number "three hundred and twenty" is a slightly inaccurate rendering of the Roman Senate's membership (actually ~300); it is preserved as written.

**On "one man each year" (v.16):** This refers to the Roman consuls — two men, not one. The author apparently did not know (or did not convey) the dual consulship. The text says "one man" (*hena andra*) and this is what should be translated, not corrected.

**On the treaty text (vv.22-32):** The treaty is formally introduced as an official document inscribed on bronze tablets. It is in the standard form of Roman-era treaties (*foedera*). The formal treaty language should be rendered with appropriate legal register.

**On "by sea and by land" (v.32):** This formula — *kata thalassan kai kata gen* — is the standard expression of unlimited military commitment in Hellenistic treaties. All translators preserve it. No disagreement.

---

1. Judas heard of the fame of the Romans — that they were very powerful, that they welcomed all who came to them, and that they made treaties of friendship with all who put themselves in their hands.
2. He was told of their wars and the brave deeds they had done in Galatia, how they had conquered the Galatians and made them subject to tribute.
3. He heard what they had done in Spain to gain control of the silver and gold mines there,
4. and how through planning and persistence they had taken possession of the whole region, even though it lay very far from them. They had crushed kings who marched against them from the ends of the earth, inflicted defeat on them; and the rest were paying tribute to Rome year after year.
5. Philip and Perseus, king of the Macedonians, and all who had raised arms against them were defeated and brought under their authority.
6. Antiochus the Great, king of Asia, had come against them with one hundred and twenty elephants, cavalry, chariots, and a very great army — and he too was defeated.
7. They took him alive and decreed that he and the kings who reigned after him should pay a heavy tribute, give hostages, and surrender a parcel of their territory:
8. the regions of India, Media, and Lydia, and some of the finest lands they held — which they took and gave to King Eumenes.
9. The Greeks had once plotted to come and destroy them.
10. But the Romans got word of it, sent a single commander against them, and he fought them: many of them fell, their women and children were taken captive, they were plundered, their strongholds torn down, and they were reduced to subjection — as they remain to this day.
11. All the other kingdoms and islands that had ever risen against them were likewise destroyed and made subject;
12. but with their friends and those who relied on them they maintained their friendship faithfully. They became masters over kingdoms near and far, and all who heard their name stood in awe of them.
13. Those whom they wish to make kings, they make kings; and those whom they wish to remove, they remove; and they were very greatly exalted.
14. And yet, for all this, not one of them put on a crown, nor did any clothe himself in purple to make himself great.
15. They had established a senate, and every day three hundred and twenty men sat in council, deliberating perpetually over public affairs, to govern the people well.
16. They entrust their government to one man each year to rule over all their territory, and everyone obeys that one man; and there is no envy or jealousy among them.
17. Judas chose Eupolemus son of John son of Accos, and Jason son of Eleazar, and sent them to Rome to establish a treaty of friendship and alliance,
18. and to obtain relief from the yoke — for they could see that the kingdom of the Greeks was reducing Israel to complete slavery.
19. They made the very long journey to Rome and entered the senate house. They arose and said:
20. "Judas Maccabeus, his brothers, and the Jewish people have sent us to you to make with you a treaty of alliance and peace, and to enroll us among your allies and friends."
21. The proposal was well received by the senate.
22. This is a copy of the letter they wrote on bronze tablets and sent to Jerusalem to be kept there as a lasting record of peace and alliance:
23. "May all go well with the Romans and with the Jewish nation by sea and by land, forever; may sword and enemy be far from them.
24. If war comes first against Rome, or against any of her allies throughout all her dominion,
25. the Jewish nation shall fight alongside them wholeheartedly, as the situation requires.
26. To those who are making war, they shall not give or supply grain, weapons, silver, or ships; this is Rome's decision; and they shall fulfill these obligations without receiving any payment in return.
27. In the same way, if war comes first against the Jewish nation, the Romans shall fight alongside them wholeheartedly, as the situation requires;
28. and grain, weapons, silver, or ships shall not be given to those making war against them; this is Rome's decision; and they shall fulfill these terms without guile.
29. On these terms the Romans make this covenant with the Jewish people.
30. But if hereafter either side decides to add to or subtract from these terms, they shall do so at their own discretion; and whatever they add or subtract shall be valid and binding.
31. Regarding the wrongs which King Demetrius is inflicting upon you, we have written to him as follows: 'Why have you made your yoke so heavy upon our friends and allies the Jews?
32. If therefore they bring any further complaint against you, we will take up their cause and make war against you by sea and by land.'"
